title: Simple Sorting
description: Bubble Sort and Selection Sort: how they rearrange data, why they're both O(n²), and where they still make sense.

sections.title: Introduction to Algorithmic Sorting
sections.content:
Sorting rearranges data into ascending or descending order -- a near-mandatory prerequisite for fast search and clean database queries.

An e-commerce backend sorts products by price; a trading platform sorts transactions by timestamp. Sorted data unlocks fast searches like Binary Search; unsorted data is stuck with O(n) linear scans.

Production systems usually reach for O(n log n) sorts (Timsort, Merge Sort). This lesson covers the simpler, slower O(n²) ones -- Bubble Sort and Selection Sort -- because their mechanics (nested loops, in-place swapping) are the foundation everything else builds on.

sections.title: The Strategic Value of Organized Data
sections.content:
Searching 1,000,000 unsorted records for a string: up to 1,000,000 checks. Sorted (alphabetized) first: ~20 checks with a logarithmic search.

Every sorting algorithm boils down to the same three moves:
bullets: **Compare:** check two elements against each other.
**Validate:** decide if the current order is wrong.
**Repeat:** keep passing over the data until nothing's out of order.

sections.title: Algorithm Profile: Bubble Sort
sections.content:
Bubble Sort compares each pair of adjacent elements and swaps them if they're in the wrong order (e.g. left > right for ascending).

That repeated local swapping pushes the largest remaining value steadily rightward -- by the end of one full pass, the single largest value is guaranteed to be in its correct final spot.

Since each pass locks one more element in place at the end, the next pass can ignore it -- the unsorted region shrinks by one each time, until nothing's left to sort.

sections.title: Algorithm Profile: Selection Sort
sections.content:
Instead of swapping constantly, Selection Sort splits the array into a sorted left side and unsorted right side, and does just one swap per pass.

It scans the whole unsorted region for the minimum (or maximum) value, tracking its *index* as it goes -- not swapping yet. Once the scan finishes, it swaps that extremum into place at the boundary.

One swap per pass, versus Bubble Sort's many -- far less memory writing, same overall O(n²) time.

sections.title: Execution Trace: The Single Pass Invariant
sections.content:
**Bubble Sort**, one pass on `[5, 2, 8, 1]` (ascending):
1. Compare 5, 2 → swap → `[2, 5, 8, 1]`.
2. Compare 5, 8 → no swap → `[2, 5, 8, 1]`.
3. Compare 8, 1 → swap → `[2, 5, 1, 8]`.
**Result:** the max (8) is now locked in the last slot. The unsorted region shrinks to the first three elements.

**Selection Sort**, same array:
1. Assume index 0 (`5`) is the min.
2. Scan `[2, 8, 1]` -- the true min is `1` at index 3.
3. Swap index 0 and index 3.
**Result:** `[1, 2, 8, 5]` -- one swap, `1` locked in, sorted boundary advances by one.

sections.title: Architectural Implementation in Python
sections.content:
The outer loop tracks the shrinking unsorted boundary; the inner loop does the scanning and comparing.

Bubble Sort's inner loop stops at `len(arr) - pass_index - 1` to skip already-sorted elements. Selection Sort's inner loop tracks an index (`min_idx`), not values, deferring the actual swap until the scan is done.

Flipping `>` to `<` flips ascending to descending.

sections.title: Mathematical Complexity and Quadratic Constraints
sections.content:
Both algorithms nest a nearly-full loop inside another, degrading to **O(n²)**.

Why: pass 1 does ~n comparisons, pass 2 does n-1, pass 3 does n-2, and so on down to 1. That sum is n(n-1)/2 -- drop the constants and lower terms, and you're left with O(n²).

At n=10,000, that's ~50,000,000 iterations. Timsort (O(n log n)) solves the same array in ~132,000.

Both are still **O(1) auxiliary space** -- no new arrays, just in-place swaps via temp pointers.

sections.title: Architectural Trade-offs: Sorting vs. Searching
sections.content:
Sorting restructures data; searching just scans it -- and sorting is expensive enough that it's worth asking whether it's justified.

Running thousands of repeated queries against a static dataset? Pay the one-time O(n log n) sort to unlock O(log n) searches forever after -- a clear win.

Just one lookup on data that changes constantly? Sorting first (O(n log n) or worse) just to search once is a net loss -- a plain O(n) linear search wins.

subsections.title: Engineering Merits
bullets: **Stable (Bubble Sort):** equal elements keep their original order.

subsections.title: System Vulnerabilities
bullets: **Bubble Sort writes a lot** -- heavy swap overhead.
**Not adaptive** -- doesn't notice data that's already mostly sorted.

sections.title: Real-World Integration Constraints
sections.content:
Enterprise backends avoid these entirely -- O(n²) is a nonstarter at scale.

But in embedded systems (microcontrollers, IoT sensors) with arrays of maybe 10-20 items and tight memory, Selection Sort's low overhead can genuinely beat a recursive Merge Sort's setup cost.

Mostly, though, they're the standard teaching tool -- a hands-on way to see nested loops turn into real runtime cost before moving to faster algorithms.

subsections.title: Vulnerability: Assuming Single Pass Resolution
subsections.content: One pass only locks in the extreme value at the boundary -- the rest of the array still needs more passes.

subsections.title: Vulnerability: Redundant Boundary Scanning
subsections.content: Skip the `- pass_index` shrink on the inner loop and you'll keep re-checking elements that are already sorted -- not wrong, just wasteful.

subsections.title: Vulnerability: Value Swapping vs. Pointer Indirection
subsections.content: Swapping during Selection Sort's scan itself turns it into a clumsy Bubble Sort. Track the index (`min_idx`), swap once, after the scan.

subsections.title: Vulnerability: Disregarding Quadratic Reality
subsections.content: Looks instant at n=10. Extrapolating that to production data without checking the actual complexity is how you get a slow system.

sections.title: Key Engineering Takeaways
bullets: **Bubble Sort** swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs continuously.
**Selection Sort** finds the extremum first, swaps once per pass.
The **Single Pass Invariant**: one pass locks the extreme value into its final spot.
Both are **O(n²)** worst-case and average-case time.
Both are **O(1)** auxiliary space -- safe, in-place mutation.
